1:
Everyone who assesses the counsel judges it sound, which is what makes it terrible. Ellicott says the rising's success depended on striking at once, and thinks the counsellor probably right that a man in David's distress could not have met a sudden onset; the proof is the trouble Hushai took to defeat it and the haste with which word was sent to David. Clarke puts the same judgement as a counterfactual: twelve thousand picked men falling on an unprepared camp would have settled the kingdom, and nothing short of God's miraculous interposition could have saved the little troop. Gill fills in the condition the plan relied on, a man weary with travelling and grief, trying to sleep, surprised before he could put himself in any posture of defence. Ellicott thinks the next clause too weakly rendered: what is meant is a band thrown into panic by a night attack, in whose confusion the king would be easily secured. Henry describes the strategy and then names it: the war shut into a little compass by fighting neither small nor great but the king only, and ended in a little time — smite the shepherd and the sheep scatter. Ellicott alone raises a difficulty of timing: the phrase about this night is usually taken of the day David left Jerusalem, while other verses put him already at the fords of Jordan, further than a single day's march.

The promise attached to the plan is where the flattery lies. Gill explains that bringing back all the people means not capturing David's men, whom the plan would let escape, but reducing the whole nation to Absalom's obedience at a stroke. Clarke states the arithmetic of it: secure the one man and all Israel comes over, since he is the soul of the whole. Ellicott hears the assumption buried in the phrase, that Absalom is already the rightful king and David's followers have only to be brought back to their allegiance. Henry's comment is on the last word of the speech: the peace promised is the peace of a general ruin, which is how usurpers talk, and the peace of the devil's palace while the strong man armed keeps it. He sets beside it the counsel of Caiaphas against the Son of David, that one man should die for the people, and the parable of killing the heir to get the inheritance — both counsels turned into foolishness.

That the plan was accepted surprises them less than who accepted it. Gill allows the scheme was well contrived and that nothing serves a villainous design like speed, finds the son's readiness to kill an indulgent father explicable only by ambition, and is more astonished at the elders, who voted the death of a prince that had ruled them with justice and clemency, fought their battles, and raised the nation to a glory it never had. Henry notices a decorum this rebellion abandoned, since men who quarrel with crowned heads usually profess to be against the evil counsellors only, on the maxim that the king himself can do no wrong — where this proposal names the king and nobody else, and the son was not embarrassed enough to pretend to flinch at it; and he asks what good can stand before the heat of a furious ambition. Wesley repeats the same contrast almost in Henry's words, a wretch aiming at his father's throat being no wonder where the people joining him is amazing, and adds two things of his own: that the finger of God was in it, and that parents and princes so injured may remember how David had provoked God to turn against him. Keil and Delitzsch close with the fact that saves the story: the advice pleased both the son and the elders present, and he sent for Hushai all the same.
5:
That the second counsellor was called at all is where three of the voices put the weight. Gill observes that he does not seem to have been at the council board, and that whether he had yet been admitted to it is uncertain; what strikes him is the providence in a prince's wanting another opinion when the first had been approved on all hands, and wanting it from a man notoriously David's intimate friend, not settled in the new interest and no sworn adherent as the other was. Gill will ascribe that to nothing but the will of God, set on defeating the first counsel, and to a providence that blinded the prince's mind at the one point where clear sight would have served him. Ellicott states the same facts without the theology: the counsel was approved at once by the prince and the people, and yet at so important a crisis he sent for his father's other famous adviser. Wesley makes the inability to rest in good advice the providence itself, since the man whose counsel was sought had neither an equal reputation for wisdom nor any proof of loyalty to show, and his conclusion is that there is no contending with a God who can arm a man against himself and destroy him by his own mistakes and passions. Gill supplies the two small stage directions, the arrival in what was very probably the council chamber, and the leave given to speak freely.

The opening sentence of the reply is more careful than it looks. Keil and Delitzsch give it plainly, that the advice Ahithophel has given this time is not good, with the explanation following. Ellicott would move the phrase about this time to the front of the sentence, so that it reads as a judgement on this occasion only — which concedes that the same man's earlier advice had been wise, and so puts on an appearance of candour.

The description of the father and his men is the first argument, and it answers the first counsel point for point. Keil and Delitzsch render them heroes of a ferocious disposition, like a bear robbed of her young in the open field, with the father himself a man of war who will not spend the night among the people — which is to say that the plan of coming on him unawares and killing him will not work. They also reject a proposed reading that would make the verb mean he does not let the people lodge for the night, on the ground that it will not square with the verse following. Gill points the contradiction out explicitly, that these are men of courage and valour and not the weak-handed and faint-hearted troops the first counsellor had described. Clarke takes the figure literally enough to comment on it, noting that all wild beasts are furious when robbed of their young and that there are remarkable instances of the she-bear's affection in such a case, one of which he promises at the end of the chapter.
9:
The argument from the hiding places draws on David's own history. Gill notes that the man had learned every lurking place in the land while escaping Saul, and that concealment was not the whole danger: lying hidden with picked men, he might start out when the moment offered and fall on the pursuing troops unawares. Wesley takes the same line and carries it one step further, to the effect such a first success would have — a small defeat at the outset would animate David's men to push on and dishearten the larger army, and so be both a presage and a cause of its total rout.

The melting of the brave is the next stroke, and Gill is willing to name the man it was aimed at. Whoever heard that part of the new army had been cut up would lose heart however lion-like his temper, and the counsellor himself, for all his boasted courage, would melt like water at such a rebuff on first setting out. Gill then turns aside into the lore of the animal: the lion is proverbial for courage as much as strength, some derive its Hebrew name from the word for heart, and a poet gives Hercules a lion's heart — yet Leo Africanus reports African lions so naturally timid that they run from the cry of children, particularly at one place, which made it a proverb in Fez to call a blustering coward a lion of that town.

The counter-plan itself is short, and its motives are the interesting part. Keil and Delitzsch render it as a general muster from Dan to Beersheba, numerous as the sand by the sea, with the prince going into the war in his own person, and they note that the early translators confused the word for war with another. Ellicott describes the difficulty the speaker faced, having to make the worse appear the better reason against a man famous for wisdom and plainly devoted to the new interest, while his own loyalty had only just been questioned. On Ellicott's account he managed it by pressing every hazard and contingency in the first plan and offering one with no risk in it at all, which works only on the assumption that the mass of Israel was already and would remain on the prince's side — an assumption he flatters his hearer by taking for granted. Wesley separates the pretence from the design: the pretence was slow work but sure, and the design was to buy David time to raise an army and make provision, and to let the people's heat cool until they bethought themselves of their duty and returned to their allegiance. On the invitation to command in person Wesley adds two inducements that have nothing to do with war, that soldiers fight harder when the man who distributes rewards and punishments is watching them, and that the glory of the victory would then be wholly the prince's, where the other counsellor had been angling to keep it for himself.
12:
The image of the dew is doing two jobs at once. Gill takes it for the practical advantage of numbers, since an army spread abroad could hardly fail to find a man who might easily lie concealed from twelve thousand. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as letting themselves down on him as the dew falls on the earth, and argue for that verb against the alternative of reading the word as a contracted pronoun, which would call for a different construction; the verb they prefer is used of an army encamping and of flies and grasshoppers settling in swarms. Wesley reads the figure for its four qualities, that dew falls plenteously, suddenly, irresistibly and on every side at once.

The threat about the city is where the speech turns extravagant, and all of them say so. Gill explains the case it covers, a man who has given up the open country for a fortified place and means to hold out in it. Keil and Delitzsch render the boast as ropes laid to the city and the whole of it dragged down to the brook, with not so much as a pebble left; they note the brook because fortified towns were generally built on heights, and they call the whole thing hyperbole about the nation's irresistible strength, calculated to make the advice sound more plausible. Clarke doubts the word for ropes is being used in its ordinary sense, since no city could be pulled down with cables, and prefers the Chaldee, which he thinks should be the best judge here and which renders it towers. Ellicott agrees it is deliberate hyperbole about united Israel and adds what it was for, since such talk pleased the prince's vanity and dazzled his imagination. Wesley's gloss is the same, that the expression suited an insolent young man's vainglorious temper, and either promised to do this if he could not be destroyed another way or claimed they would be numerous enough to do it if the occasion arose; and the river in the sentence is the one adjoining the city, towns being usually built near water for defence and convenience.

The vote goes the way the speech was aimed, and the narrator explains why. Gill identifies the voters as the elders who had approved the first counsel. Keil and Delitzsch say the advice was preferred because it had been built to be preferred, and they quote Clericus to the effect that it looked safe and was full of a kind of boasting that pleased the younger men. Their own analysis is sharper: everything said about the bravery of David and his men was true, and the deception lay in the assumption that the whole nation from Dan to Beersheba would gather as one man around the prince — when it might easily have been foreseen that once the first excitement of the revolution cooled, a large part of the people and the army would go back to David. That possibility, they observe, never entered the heads of the prince or his supporters. Wesley closes on the providence rather than the policy, with the comfort that God turns all men's hearts as the rivers of water, stands in the congregation of the mighty, keeps an overruling hand in all counsels and a negative voice in all resolves, and laughs at men's projects against his children.
15:
The warning is sent because nobody trusts the vote to hold. Gill has him go straight from the council to the two priests he knew were in David's interest and through whom he was to pass on whatever happened in the city. Keil and Delitzsch give the message as both counsels reported and an urgent instruction not to spend the night by the fords of the desert but to cross at once, lest the king and all his people be destroyed; they weigh two readings of the clause about destruction, either a devouring coming on the king or, supplying the subject, the crossing being cut off from him, and reject a third. Henry supplies the reasoning: the messenger could not be sure the first counsel would not be taken up again, perhaps having been dismissed before the decision was reached, or fearing the council would change its mind — and either way it was good to provide against the worst. Ellicott says the same, that the advice was accepted for the moment but could easily be exchanged, so the Jordan had to be put between the king and the rebels at once. Wesley adds only the mechanism he feared, that minds would change and the first counsellor would get his pursuit after all.

Getting the news out was the difficulty. Keil and Delitzsch place the two young men, sons of the priests, at the Rogel spring outside the walls, with a maid of one high priest carrying the message out, since they dared not be seen coming in; after what had happened publicly, nobody could doubt where the high priests stood. Gill explains that the pair had not gone back into Jerusalem with their fathers but waited by their direction at this place, which the Targum calls the fuller's fountain, from the treading of clothes with the feet. Clarke derives the name the same way, from words for a well and a foot. Ellicott puts it just outside the city on the border between Benjamin and Judah, and reports two candidate sites, the Fountain of the Virgin on the western slope of the Kidron valley and Job's Well below the junction of Kidron and Hinnom, the second fitting the description in Joshua much better, though either suits this passage. His observation about the choice of spot is the shrewdest in the chapter: women came to the fountains for water, so messages could be passed there without attracting notice. Henry reads it as a judgement on the city, since things went ill with Jerusalem when two such faithful priests could not be seen entering it.

The messenger herself attracts comment out of all proportion to her sentence. Henry calls her a poor simple young woman who probably came to the well on pretence of fetching water, and allows that a spoken message risked being garbled, with the reflection that providence can make an ignorant girl a trusty courier and serve its wise counsels by the foolish things of the world. Wesley gives her the same pretext, water or washing. Ellicott notes the definite article, probably pointing to some well-known maid of the high priest's household, and that the English word for her occurs nowhere else in the Bible. Clarke makes that the occasion of a long note, insisting the Hebrew means simply girl or maid-servant and the English word has no business in the verse. He canvasses derivations from Anglo-Saxon, Belgic and Gothic, tracks the word through the English versions — Coverdale's damsel, Becke's and Cardmarden's with the word he objects to, a maid in Barker's — and suspects King James of restoring it himself, as he is said to have restored another homely word elsewhere. Clarke's closing complaint is one a translator would recognise, that the same Hebrew term is rendered handmaid, bondmaid, maiden, womanservant, maidservant and servant in other places, with the same latitude taken in innumerable instances.
18:
The couriers are spotted almost at once. Gill has a lad see them talking with the girl and then setting off for David's army, and reports Josephus for a different version, in which horsemen noticed them a quarter of a mile outside Jerusalem and carried word back. Keil and Delitzsch suppose spies had been set to watch the priests and their sons, which is why a servant was in a position to see anything; and they have the two young men, once they knew they were observed, hurry into a house at Bahurim whose courtyard held a well, or a cistern dry at that season, and climb down into it.

The hiding is described with a care that interests all four voices. Keil and Delitzsch have the man's wife take the covering she had close at hand, lay it over the mouth of the cistern, and scatter peeled barley on top so that nothing could be noticed; they commend the Latin version for explaining the point of it, that she looked as though she were drying the grain. Gill identifies her as the householder's wife, following Abarbinel, and keeps the detail that the cloth hid the fact that there was a well there at all. Ellicott glosses the grain itself, a word found in only one other passage, meaning wheat or barley beaten or ground to take off the hull and then spread out to dry. Wesley draws the inference the scene allows, that drying grain in the sun puts the episode in summer.

The lie that follows is recorded by everyone and judged by only some. Gill has the pursuers arrive with intelligence of the road taken and the house entered, so the question put to the woman was not a guess. Keil and Delitzsch give her answer, that the men had gone over the little water-brook, and the result, that the searchers were led wrong and did not find them. Ellicott notes that her word for brook occurs nowhere else, that some writers take it for a proper name, and that a small brook of the same name is said to exist in that neighbourhood still. He then sets the episode beside the two other occasions where a woman deceived pursuers to save a man, and observes that the historian records what was done without comment of any kind. Wesley is not willing to leave it there: the brook meant the Jordan, and the statement was a manifest lie.
21:
The crossing is reported in a few words and noticed for one detail. Keil and Delitzsch have the young men come up out of the cistern once the searchers had gone, carry the warning to cross at once, and the whole company over Jordan in haste, with the narrator's tally that by daybreak not one man was missing. Gill adds that in crossing at all David was taking Hushai's advice. Henry cannot say whether they used ferryboats, which probably always plied there, or the fords, but fastens on the tally: nobody deserted in a distress that great, nobody stayed behind sick or weary, and nobody was lost in the water. He thinks the line makes the king a figure of the Messiah, who could say in his own difficult day that of all given him he had lost none.

The suicide is explained by four voices, and they divide between calculation and wounded pride. Keil and Delitzsch make it foresight: the counsellor could see that the cause would be lost through the rejection of his plan and that it would then be all over with him, so he went home, set his house in order and hanged himself — in which they find David's earlier prayer answered. Ellicott says the same and puts the end plainly, that the man was shrewd enough to see the rebellion would fail with this delay and that a traitor's death was waiting for him. Clarke refuses the plea of madness, since every step was deliberate, and his verdict is the harshest in the chapter: a man who would neither watch the ruin he had foreseen nor look for mercy from the king, a very bad man who died an unprepared and accursed death. Henry puts the weight on the slight instead. A judgement that had always swayed the council board was now set below another man's, and the proud heart could not carry the affront; the longer he turned it over the more violent the resentment grew, until he resolved not to live to see another preferred. Henry's sharpest sentence is that all men thought him a wise man and he thought himself the only wise man, so that he would die and let wisdom die with him. His moral is that those who think too well of themselves are their own worst enemies, and that what will break a proud man's heart would not break a humble man's sleep.

The deliberateness is what Henry keeps returning to. The thing was not done in a heat: the man rode home to his own city and his own house to do it, took time to consider, and did it anyway; and to prove himself in his senses he first put his household in order, made his will and settled his accounts — yet the sense that managed all that could not revoke the sentence his pride had passed on his own neck, or even suspend it until the campaign's outcome was known. Henry's two summary sentences, that contempt was here poured on the wisdom of man and honour done to the justice of God when the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands, reappear almost word for word in Wesley's note on the verse. Henry adds a tradition from Dr. Lightfoot, that the fifty-fifth psalm was written about this man's part in the plot, and that he is the equal, guide and acquaintance complained of there. He also reckons the death a gain to David's cause, since a man who had swallowed the affront and stayed at the prince's elbow might have given advice of pernicious consequence later. The last detail is the burial: it was evidently not then the custom to dishonour the bodies of self-murderers, for he was laid in his father's sepulchre, though Henry thinks he deserved no better than the burial of an ass.
24:
The two armies are placed before the battle is described. Gill identifies the king's refuge as a city beyond Jordan in the tribe of Gad, remembered as the place where the angels of God met Jacob and as Ishbosheth's seat for a time. Keil and Delitzsch add that it was probably fortified and stood near the ford of the Jabbok, and Ellicott draws the obvious inference, that whatever had recommended it as a capital to the house of Saul recommended it now as a refuge and a rallying point. On the other side, Keil and Delitzsch have the prince cross the river with all the fighting men gathered on Hushai's plan and encamp in Gilead, and Wesley marks the delay in it, since the crossing waited until the whole muster was complete. Gill locates Gilead among Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, and has the rebel army pitch there to offer battle. Ellicott describes the region more fully, the tract east of Jordan running from Moab in the south to Bashan in the north with a river valley for its probable northern boundary, and notes both that the site of Mahanaim has never been identified and that the prince never reached it, being met and beaten before he could.

The new commander is introduced by his relations. Gill observes simply that the old one was away with David, and Keil and Delitzsch spell out why that mattered, since Joab had stayed loyal and gone with his king. Ellicott puts the appointment as a choice of the nearest available substitute, the prince's own cousin. Clarke states the kinship as a pair of sisters' children, both of them nephews to David, and Keil and Delitzsch make the relation an illegitimate one, Amasa's father having seduced the sister of Joab's mother.

The genealogy in this verse is a tangle, and two of them work at it. Keil and Delitzsch find the description of the father as an Israelite striking, since there was no reason to say so of anybody in this family, and they reject the Greek reading that makes him a man of Jezreel, where one of David's wives came from, as mere conjecture. Their own conclusion is that the true reading is Ishmaelite, on the authority of the parallel in Chronicles, where the name appears in a contracted form. Ellicott reaches the same result by the same route, treating the two forms of the name as one name and the word Israelite as probably an error, and he reports that the Greek copies disagree between themselves, one having Ishmaelite and the other Jezreelite. On the mother he sets out the difficulty without solving it: she is called here the sister of Joab's mother, while Chronicles makes both women sisters of Jesse's sons, so that either sister must mean half-sister or else Nahash, ordinarily a man's name, was the name of Jesse's wife. Ellicott says it is impossible to decide, and adds that the Jewish tradition identifying Nahash with Jesse himself has nothing to support it.
27:
The narrative pauses to name three men, and two of the commentators work on the first of them. Ellicott treats the pause as deliberate, an account of the help that reached the king while the rebel muster was still being gathered. On Shobi he offers two possibilities: that after dismantling the Ammonite capital David had left a brother of the late king as governor of the conquered territory, who now came forward out of gratitude and fidelity, or that this was simply the son of some Israelite of the same name living in the captured city. Keil and Delitzsch give the same alternatives and add the general point, that these were wealthier citizens of the country east of Jordan, and that their help is recorded as the first sign that the people had not all fallen away and that some men of standing were still firm. Wesley takes a third line, that this Ammonite had disliked and disowned the outrage done to David's ambassadors and had been left as king or governor of the remnant when the rest were destroyed. Ellicott's note on the second name is shorter and sharper, that David was now reaping the return of his kindness to the crippled son of Jonathan.

The inventory is treated as evidence about how people lived. Gill explains why bedding headed the list, since men who had fled Jerusalem in haste could bring none and had been badly provided in the wilderness, and he reports the Greek version's detail that there were ten of them, of tapestry worked on both sides as the ancients used, with ten basins to match. Keil and Delitzsch content themselves with the list as it stands. Clarke takes each article in turn: the beds were no doubt skins of beasts, mats and carpets; the basons probably wooden bowls of the kind the Arabs still eat out of and knead bread in; the earthen vessels probably clay baked in the sun, for drawing water and boiling whatever needed cooking. He also notices what is missing, since there is no direct mention of meat, little of it being eaten in that country and none of it keeping, and he will not say whether the sheep were brought for flesh or for milk. Gill adds a note on two of the later items, that honey was much in use among the ancients, appearing in Homer among the provisions of a feast and as food that children were raised on, that the old Scythians lived on milk and honey, and that honey and butter were much of the ordinary diet in Judea.

The parched barley sets Clarke off on the longest digression in the chapter. He cites Mr. Jones for the Moors of west Barbary, who make the flour of parched barley their chief provision for a journey and use it at home as well, carrying it in a leathern satchel; the satchels are ordinarily goat-skins, and Clarke describes one lying in front of him as he writes. It had been drawn off the animal whole before the carcase was cut up, the openings at the fore-legs and the tail elegantly closed and fitted with leather thongs for slinging it over the back of a man, an ass or a camel, the neck left open with a running string to draw it shut like a purse, and the skin itself tanned. Ellicott's contribution to the verse is a textual one: the last item in the list is a word found nowhere else and of uncertain meaning, where the English follows the Chaldee and the rabbinic interpretation while the Latin makes it fat calves and a Greek version sucking calves. Wesley ends the chapter on the providence in it, that God sometimes makes up to his people from strangers the comfort they are disappointed of in their own families.
